source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5710229 (publisher's version, JAMA Psychiatry 2017;74(9):911-923, courtesy of the AMA), read in full in my own browser tab: key points, abstract, introduction, methods, results with Tables 1-5, discussion including Limitations and Strengths, conclusions, article notes (affiliations, funding, conflicts) and references.

claims.overstatement: The figures are not overstated. The trend sentence ('these studies cannot show whether the disorder became more common') understates this paper's own conclusion and does not say so. The authors report a significant 49.4% rise in DSM-IV AUD, call it a public health crisis, and defend the comparison: identical alcohol-use questions; near-identical AUD items (kappa 0.97-0.98); nonresponse weighting; and agreement with other indicators. The editors' caution is defensible: the response rates were 81.0% vs 60.0/60.1%, the designs differed, and this paper never mentions the stable NSDUH AUD figure that Grant et al. 2015 reported while citing NSDUH for alcohol use. But the claim should label the caution as the editors' appraisal and give the authors' view and their checks. The heavy-drinking amounts appear as the study's definition (tied to the US dietary guidelines) and do not read as advice.
claims.note: Numbers checked: Table 3 total 8.5 (8.0-8.9) and 12.7 (12.1-13.3); Table 4 total 12.9 (printed 12.3-17.5) and 17.5 (16.7-18.3); Table 5 total 46.5 (44.3-48.7) and 54.5 (52.7-56.4); response 81.0% and 60.0% (Methods), 60.1% (Limitations); 4+/5+ standard drinks of 14 g, exceeded at least weekly. Recomputed: the difference is 12.7-8.5 = 4.2 points, the same as the editors' figure, and 4.2/8.5 = 49.4%, matching the paper. The other two changes are 35.7% and 17.2%, also matching the paper. The 2001-2002 interval for people who drank, 12.3-17.5, is implausible: its upper half-width is 4.6 against 0.6-0.8 elsewhere, so I agree it is a misprint. The components multiply to 81.1% (NESARC: 98.5 x 88.5 x 93.0) and 60.5% (NESARC-III: 72.0 x 84.0), against the printed 81.0% and 60.0/60.1%; this is immaterial. 'Lay interviewers' is supported here: interviewers were not clinicians, and a validation substudy found prevalence and concordance similar to clinician diagnoses. 'Partly' refers only to the trend inference; every figure the claim takes from this paper is correct. Funding: sponsored by NIAAA with supplemental NIDA funding and NIH grant K05AA014223; 9 of 11 authors at NIAAA's Epidemiology and Biometry Branch; conflicts: none reported.

anchors.extracted: NESARC-III: face-to-face survey of 36 309 US adults aged 18+ in households and selected group quarters, multistage probability sample, April 2012 to June 2013; household response 72.0%, person 84.0%, overall 60.0%; weighted for oversampling and nonresponse to the 2012 American Community Survey.

2001-2002 NESARC: face-to-face survey of 43 093 adults, April 2001 to June 2002. Primary sampling units were counties or county equivalents; black people, Hispanic people and young adults were oversampled. Response: sampling frame 98.5%, household 88.5%, person 93.0%, overall 81.0%. Weighted to the 2000 Census; reviewed by the US Census Bureau and OMB. The sampling, oversampled groups, weighting base and field organisation differ from NESARC-III.

Alcohol-use questions identical in both surveys. High-risk drinking: 4+ standard drinks (14 g pure alcohol) on any day for women, 5+ for men, following the US dietary guidelines, exceeded at least weekly in the prior 12 months. Both surveys are NIAAA's.

anchors.locator: Results > 12-Month DSM-IV AUD, 1st paragraph; Table 3, Total row
anchors.extracted: 12-month DSM-IV AUD 8.5% (95% CI 8.0-8.9) in 2001-2002 vs 12.7% (12.1-13.3) in 2012-2013, relative change 49.4%, P<.05 (two-sided t test on SUDAAN standard errors); no absolute difference printed (4.2 points, editors' calculation).

anchors.locator: Results > 12-Month DSM-IV AUD Among 12-Month Alcohol Users, 1st paragraph; Table 4, Total row
anchors.extracted: AUD among people who drank in the past year: 12.9% (interval printed as 12.3-17.5) in 2001-2002 vs 17.5% (16.7-18.3) in 2012-2013, change 35.7%. The same interval is printed in the abstract.

anchors.locator: Results > 12-Month DSM-IV AUD Among 12-Month High-Risk Drinkers, 1st paragraph; Table 5, Total row
anchors.extracted: AUD among people with high-risk drinking 46.5% (44.3-48.7) in 2001-2002 vs 54.5% (52.7-56.4) in 2012-2013, change 17.2%.

No biological testing. Homeless and incarcerated people not covered in either survey, possibly underestimating drinking and AUD. Interviewers were not clinicians, but a NESARC-III validation substudy found prevalence and concordance similar to clinician diagnoses. Response 60.1% vs 81.0%; the authors say weighting for nonresponse made the surveys comparable and agreement with other studies supports the increases.

DSM-IV items virtually identical (3 reworded, 3 abuse questions added in NESARC-III). Prevalence with and without the added questions: NESARC 8.5% vs 8.2% (kappa 0.97); NESARC-III 12.7% vs 12.2% (kappa 0.98). The authors conclude the item differences did not cause the change.

anchors.locator: Abstract > Conclusions and Relevance; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusions
anchors.extracted: The authors conclude that AUD rose 49.4% (about 17.6 million to 29.9 million Americans, their estimate) and call this a public health crisis. They support it with other trends: alcohol use +6.0% (NHIS) and +9.1% (NSDUH), 5+ drinks +17.8% (NHIS), per-capita sales +6.4%, and alcohol-related morbidity and mortality. NSDUH's AUD prevalence is not mentioned. Conclusions: treatment rates under 10%.

anchors.locator: Article notes > Funding/Support, Role of the Funder/Sponsor, Conflict of Interest Disclosures; author affiliations
anchors.extracted: Sponsored by NIAAA with supplemental NIDA funding and NIH grant K05AA014223 (Hasin). Nine of 11 authors at NIAAA's Epidemiology and Biometry Branch. Conflicts: none reported. The role-of-funder statement says the funders had no role in design, conduct or analysis.

key_findings.correction: Locator would be clearer named: Results > 12-Month DSM-IV AUD Among 12-Month Alcohol Users, and Results > 12-Month DSM-IV AUD Among 12-Month High-Risk Drinkers, 1st paragraph each; Tables 4 and 5.
All absolute differences recomputed from Tables 1-3; each matches.

reporting_issues.note: Upper half-width 4.6 vs lower 0.6, about 8 times; neighbouring intervals are +/-0.6 to 0.8. I did not visit the JAMA page.
Table 2 high school 9.6-11.1 vs 13.9-15.9 and some college 9.0-10.0 vs 10.9-12.4: neither has a marker and neither pair of intervals overlaps.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high for the between-survey change, with each survey's own prevalence moderate, is reasonable. The only comparability checks are identical drinking questions and the added-question test; design, response and fieldwork differences are not modelled; and NSDUH's AUD trend disagrees.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is fair: 'public health crisis' and subgroup claims rest on relative change without interaction tests; the coherence argument omits the NSDUH AUD trend; the Conclusions give treatment and cost figures not from these data.

missed: cannot_establish lists 'a $90 incentive in NESARC-III' as a difference between the surveys. The paper reports the incentive only for NESARC-III and says nothing about one in 2001-2002, so this difference is not documented here and should be marked as unknown.
